introduction: A ship caught in a terrifying storm brings a king, courtiers and servants within reach of Prospero, an exiled ruler who commands spirits on an island. His daughter Miranda knows little of the political betrayal that brought them there. As the survivors separate, Prospero directs encounters that test love, expose ambition and unsettle certainty about what is real. Ariel's desire for liberty and Caliban's resistance to service complicate his authority, while an unexpected meeting offers a different future for the children of old enemies.

fullSynopsis.text: A tempest throws the ship carrying Alonso, King of Naples, and his companions into apparent ruin. On a nearby island, Miranda begs her father Prospero to end the suffering. He assures her that no one has been harmed and explains their past: his brother Antonio took Milan from him with Alonso's support twelve years earlier. Prospero and the young Miranda were abandoned at sea, but Gonzalo secretly supplied necessities and books. Now fortune has brought his enemies within reach, and Prospero has ordered the spirit Ariel to create the storm and scatter the passengers safely around the island.

Ariel seeks the freedom Prospero has promised. Prospero reminds him of his rescue from the tree in which the witch Sycorax imprisoned him and threatens renewed confinement before promising release. Sycorax's son Caliban also serves Prospero unwillingly. Caliban claims the island through his mother and says Prospero has dispossessed him; Prospero justifies confinement by Caliban's attempted assault on Miranda, which Caliban acknowledges. Ariel's music draws Alonso's son Ferdinand towards Miranda. Each believes the other extraordinary, and they fall in love. Prospero welcomes the attraction privately but accuses Ferdinand of spying and imposes labour to test his love.

Elsewhere Alonso grieves for Ferdinand, whom he supposes drowned. Gonzalo tries to console him and imagines a commonwealth without labour or domination, while Antonio and Sebastian mock him. When Ariel puts most of the company to sleep, Antonio urges Sebastian to imitate his own usurpation by killing Alonso and taking Naples. They draw their swords, but Ariel wakes Gonzalo and the king, preventing the attack. Caliban meanwhile meets the jester Trinculo and drunken butler Stephano. Wine persuades him to worship Stephano as a new master, and he promises to show the island's resources in exchange for release from Prospero's service.

Miranda offers to help Ferdinand with his logs, and they promise themselves to one another while Prospero secretly watches with approval. Caliban urges Stephano to kill Prospero after seizing his books and to take Miranda and the island. Invisible Ariel provokes quarrels among the conspirators and leads them astray with music. For Alonso's party, spirits produce a banquet that vanishes when Ariel appears as a harpy. He accuses Alonso, Antonio and Sebastian of their treatment of Prospero and demands repentance. Alonso interprets Ferdinand's supposed death as punishment; the others react defiantly, and Gonzalo sends companions after the distressed men.

Prospero approves the young couple's union but requires chastity before the wedding. He gives them a spirit masque in which Iris, Ceres and Juno celebrate marriage and abundance. Remembering Caliban's conspiracy, he abruptly dismisses the entertainment and reflects on the passing of spectacle and life. Ariel has drawn the plotters through thorns and a foul pool. Outside Prospero's cell, glittering clothes distract Stephano and Trinculo despite Caliban's pleas to complete the murder first. Spirits in the shape of hounds drive all three away, and Prospero orders further painful punishment. His enemies are now entirely at his mercy.

Ariel's description of the captives' suffering moves Prospero to choose mercy. He renounces his rough magic, declaring that he will break his staff and drown his book. He restores the courtiers' senses, forgives Antonio and requires his dukedom back. Alonso asks pardon and restores Milan; Antonio gives no corresponding admission of guilt. Prospero reveals Ferdinand and Miranda together, reuniting father and son. The mariners report their ship sound. Caliban recognizes his folly, and Prospero orders him and the servants to tidy the cell as a condition of pardon. Prospero plans the next day's voyage to Naples, the lovers' wedding and his own retirement to Milan. He gives Ariel one last task of favourable weather before freedom. In the epilogue, he asks the audience's applause, breath and indulgence to release him; the voyage and marriage remain ahead.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: A royal ship struggles through a storm as the boatswain's practical authority conflicts with the passengers' rank. Miranda believes she has seen a catastrophe, but Prospero assures her that his magic has preserved everyone. He tells her how Antonio, aided by Alonso, usurped Milan and cast them away, and how Gonzalo supplied their survival. Ariel confirms that the passengers are safely dispersed and the ship hidden intact. His request for liberty prompts Prospero's account of Sycorax and a threat before another promise of freedom. Caliban protests the loss of his island and forced service. Ariel then brings Ferdinand to Miranda; they fall in love, but Prospero imposes apparent hostility and captivity.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Gonzalo tries to console Alonso for the apparent loss of Ferdinand, while Sebastian blames the king for the voyage and Antonio mocks Gonzalo's imagined commonwealth. Ariel sends most of the party to sleep, leaving Antonio and Sebastian awake. Antonio argues that Ferdinand's presumed death and Claribel's distant marriage make Sebastian's succession possible, and cites his own successful usurpation of Milan. They prepare to kill Alonso and Gonzalo, but Ariel wakes the sleepers in time. Elsewhere, Caliban mistakes Trinculo for a tormenting spirit. Trinculo shelters beneath his garment, and Stephano discovers them. After drinking Stephano's wine, Caliban transfers his allegiance to him and celebrates what he calls freedom.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Ferdinand bears Prospero's imposed labour willingly for Miranda's sake. She offers help, reveals her name against her father's instruction, and proposes marriage; he accepts. Prospero secretly observes with delight. Caliban tells Stephano how to kill Prospero, emphasizing that his books must be secured, and offers Miranda as a future queen. Ariel, invisible, disrupts their conversation and leads them after music. Alonso abandons hope of finding Ferdinand, while Antonio and Sebastian renew their murderous intention. Spirits invite the company to a banquet, which Ariel removes as a harpy, accusing the three powerful men of their wrong against Prospero. Alonso is conscience-stricken; Antonio and Sebastian threaten resistance, and Gonzalo fears what the men's distress may produce.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Prospero tells Ferdinand that the hardships were tests of love and approves his union with Miranda, warning them to remain chaste until the marriage rites. Ariel arranges a masque of spirits as Iris, Ceres and Juno, blessing love, fertility and prosperity. Prospero interrupts it when he remembers the threat to his life and explains the vanished spectacle through the transience of earthly things. Ariel reports having led Caliban, Stephano and Trinculo through thorns into a filthy pool. The conspirators approach the cell, but stolen clothing diverts the two drinkers from Caliban's plan. Prospero and Ariel set spirit hounds on them and order bodily torment, while Ariel's freedom is again promised.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Ariel's account of the captives' misery prompts Prospero to release them rather than continue vengeance. He abjures magic and announces the future destruction of staff and book. When their senses return, Alonso asks forgiveness and restores Prospero's dukedom. Prospero forgives Antonio, conceals the recent assassination plot and reveals Ferdinand with Miranda. The reunited company learns that the ship is intact. Caliban and his companions are exposed and ordered to prepare the cell in hope of pardon. Prospero offers lodging, promises to recount his history, and plans departure for Naples, a wedding and retirement to Milan. Ariel must provide favourable sailing before becoming free. The epilogue appeals to the audience for release.

framing.label: EPILOGUE
framing.summary: Prospero addresses the audience after relinquishing his charms. His dukedom has been recovered and the deceiver pardoned, but he now depends on the spectators to release him from the island. He asks for their hands in applause and their breath to fill his sails, then connects their indulgence with prayer and the forgiveness they themselves would seek. His projected journey to Naples remains dependent on this final appeal.
